# Psalm 75 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Psalm

This is a communal thanksgiving psalm that anticipates God's righteous judgment. It echoes Hannah's song (1 Samuel 2:1–10) and foreshadows Mary's Magnificat (Luke 1:46–53). Asaph leads the congregation in gratitude, then God Himself speaks in warning to the proud, and the psalm closes with confident praise and a final divine word about cutting off the horns of the wicked and exalting the righteous. Spurgeon calls it "a song of the second advent, concerning the nearness of the Judge with the cup of wrath." ([Spurgeon, Treasury of David](https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps075.php))

---

## Title and Superscription

**"For the choirmaster: To the tune of 'Do Not Destroy.' A Psalm of Asaph. A song."**

- **"Do Not Destroy" (Al-taschith):** Also used for Psalms 57–59. Spurgeon notes it may serve "as a check upon the natural fierceness of the oppressed, or a taunt for the savage foe," or as Hubbard suggests, David's maxim during Saul's persecution to "remind himself to forebear revenge." ([Spurgeon](https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps075.php))
- **Asaph:** The great singer and prophet of David and Solomon's era (1 Chronicles 15:17–19; 25:1). He writes from the congregation's perspective. ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-75/))

---

## v. 1 — "We give thanks to You, O God; we give thanks, for Your Name is near. The people declare Your wondrous works."

- **Thanksgiving repeated for emphasis:** Spurgeon says, "Stinted gratitude is ingratitude. For infinite goodness there should be measureless thanks." The doubling shows fervency and sincerity. ([Spurgeon](https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps075.php); also cited in [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-75/))
- **"Your Name is near":** God's "Name" means His character, attributes, and personal presence. Venema explains: "The name of God is said to be near, because it had come into public notice, and was in every mind and every tongue — opposed to what is unknown and obscure, which is said to be far remote." ([Spurgeon](https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps075.php))
- **God's nearness versus pagan deities:** Spurgeon contrasts: "Baal is on a journey, but Jehovah dwells in his church." God is not distant or asleep. ([Spurgeon](https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps075.php))
- **Wondrous works declare His nearness:** We thank God not only for His works but because those works proclaim that He is near. Kidner adds: "God's name is part of His self-giving: a revelation of who He is (Exodus 34:14–15) and an invitation to call upon Him (Acts 2:21)." ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-75/))
- **Gill adds:** The word "give thanks" can also mean "confess" — confessing sins and unworthiness alongside gratitude. He sees Christ Himself at the head of His people in this thanksgiving. ([Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/75.htm))

---

## v. 2 — "When I choose a time, I will judge fairly."

- **God Himself becomes the speaker:** The voice shifts abruptly from the congregation to God. This dramatic device is also found in Psalm 46:10. ([Ellicott, cited in search results](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/75.htm))
- **"When I choose a time" (the set time):** God reserves the right to choose the timing of His judgments. G. Campbell Morgan: "He acts, never too soon and never too late." Boice: "If judgment were left in our hands, we would probably let it flash out against anything that displeases us whenever we see it. But God lets evil go unchecked sometimes for a rather long time, knowing that he has appointed a proper time." ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-75/))
- **The older rendering debate:** The KJV reads "When I shall receive the congregation." The Hebrew word *mo'ed* can mean "appointed time" or "congregation" (from the tent of meeting). Gill favours "congregation" = the elect gathered to Christ, after which judgment follows. Most modern translations (NASB, NET, ESV) favour "appointed time." ([Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/75.htm); [NET Bible notes](https://netbible.org/bible/Psalms+75))
- **"I will judge fairly" (with equity):** God judges uprightly, as Abraham confessed: "the Judge of all the earth will do right" (Genesis 18:25). No injustice will be done. ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-75/); [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/75.htm))

---

## v. 3 — "When the earth and all its dwellers quake, it is I who bear up its pillars. Selah"

- **"The earth…are dissolved" (melt):** Refers to the terror and instability when anarchy, tyranny, or divine judgment shakes human institutions. Spurgeon: "When anarchy is abroad, and tyrants are in power, everything is unloosed, dissolution threatens all things, the solid mountains of government melt as wax." ([Spurgeon](https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps075.php))
- **"I bear up the pillars of it":** Even when all seems to crumble, God Himself upholds the moral and physical order. Morgan: "There may be apparent and indeed very real dissolution of all human organization and order; but the true pillars of the earth are God-established and cannot be broken down." ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-75/))
- **Gill sees an eschatological reading:** At the final judgment, earth and inhabitants melt with fear and fire (cf. 2 Peter 3:10), but Christ sustains the world from utter destruction. He also notes that Rabbi Obadiah interpreted "pillars" figuratively as the righteous, for whose sake the world is preserved. ([Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/75.htm))
- **Spurgeon's hymn echoes:** "How can I sink with such a prop / As my eternal God, / Who bears the earth's huge pillars up, / And spreads the heavens abroad." ([Spurgeon](https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps075.php))
- **Selah:** A pause for meditation on the rightness, timing, and power of God's judgments. ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-75/))

---

## v. 4 — "I say to the proud, 'Do not boast,' and to the wicked, 'Do not lift up your horn.'"

- **God addresses the proud directly:** The same divine voice continues, warning the boastful and wicked.
- **"Fools" (boastful/proud):** Thomas Watson explains: "The ungodly are spiritual fools… Better be a fool void of reason, than a fool void of grace: this is the devil's fool." Such a one refuses God's rich offer of Christ and salvation. (Cited in [Spurgeon](https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps075.php))
- **"Lift not up the horn":** The horn is a Hebrew metaphor for strength, honour, and domination (drawn from horned animals like oxen). Lifting the horn = proud self-exaltation. Boice: "Lifting one's horn against heaven is the equivalent of shaking one's fist in God's face." Poole adds: "A metaphor from untamed and stiff-necked oxen, which will not bow their heads to receive the yoke, but lift up their heads and horns to avoid it." ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-75/); [Spurgeon](https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps075.php))
- **Gill sees antichrist typology:** The horn-lifting prefigures the little horn of Daniel 7:8 and the beast with ten horns who "opens his mouth in blasphemy against God." ([Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/75.htm))

---

## v. 5 — "Do not lift up your horn against heaven or speak with an outstretched neck."

- **Double rebuke for abounding pride:** God repeats the warning, intensifying it. Spurgeon: "A word from God soon abases the lofty." ([Spurgeon](https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps075.php))
- **"Speak with a stiff neck" (outstretched neck):** The image is of an ox that refuses to bow its head to the yoke and instead thrusts its neck upward in defiance. Spurgeon: "Impudence before God is madness. The out-stretched neck of insolent pride is sure to provoke his axe. Those who carry their heads high shall find that they will be lifted yet higher, as Haman was upon the gallows which he had prepared for the righteous man." ([Spurgeon](https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps075.php))
- **Adam Clarke notes a cultural detail:** The Abyssinian kings wore a horn on their diadem; keeping it erect made them appear stiff-necked. This psalm may allude to such royal pomp. (Cited in [Spurgeon](https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps075.php))

---

## v. 6 — "For exaltation comes neither from east nor west, nor out of the desert."

- **Promotion/exaltation does not come from earthly directions:** The proud look in all directions for advancement, but in vain. Trapp: "Ambitionists used to look this way and that way how to advance themselves, but all in vain." ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-75/))
- **Why is the north omitted?** This has drawn much discussion:
  - **Caryl:** Promotion comes from the north because the Hebrew word for "north" (*tsaphon*) means "hidden" or "secret." Promotion comes from God's hidden providence, which we take no more notice of "than we do of the furthest part of the north." (Cited in [Spurgeon](https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps075.php))
  - **Perowne:** If the psalm refers to Sennacherib, the Assyrian army approached from the north; thus it would be natural to look in all directions *but* that for help. ([Spurgeon](https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps075.php))
  - **Bateman (sermon):** The north represents coldness and purity — "The pure in heart shall see God. God is the northern light that gleams over the stillness of life's night." ([Spurgeon](https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps075.php))
- **Spurgeon summarises:** "There is a God, and a providence, and things happen not by chance." Men see only human force and carnal passion, but the unseen Lord is at work behind and within the cloud. ([Spurgeon](https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps075.php))
- **NET Bible translates the direction:** "For victory does not come from the east or west, or from the wilderness" — using Palestinian/Canaanite imagery to assert universality. ([NET](https://netbible.org/bible/Psalms+75); [Bible.org / Utley](https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-75))

---

## v. 7 — "But it is God who judges; He brings down one and exalts another."

- **God is the Judge — present tense:** "Even now he is actually judging. His seat is not vacant; his authority is not abdicated; the Lord reigneth evermore." ([Spurgeon](https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps075.php))
- **"He putteth down one, and setteth up another":** This is a central biblical theme, rooted in Hannah's song (1 Samuel 2:7) and echoed in Daniel 2:21 and Luke 1:52. Spurgeon: "Empires rise and fall at his bidding. A dungeon here, and there a throne, his will assigns. Assyria yields to Babylon, and Babylon to the Medes. Kings are but puppets in his hand." ([Spurgeon](https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps075.php))
- **Gill distinguishes two realms:** God does this both in *providence* (removing kings, raising the lowly) and in *grace* (humbling the proud-hearted to submit to Christ's righteousness, and exalting the humble to be kings and priests). He also sees it in the historic shift from Jew to Gentile — stripping one and raising the other. ([Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/75.htm))
- **All success comes from God:** Meyer: "Promotions in any direction, to positions of credit, influence, or consideration, are the gift and the work of God." Even human effort, preparation, and good habits are themselves gifts from God. ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-75/))

---

## v. 8 — "For a cup is in the hand of the LORD, full of foaming wine mixed with spices. He pours from His cup, and all the wicked of the earth drink it down to the dregs."

- **The cup of wrath:** This is one of the Bible's most vivid judgment images, developed in the prophets (Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15–16, 27–28; Habakkuk 2:16; Ezekiel 23:32–34). ([Ellicott, search excerpt](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/75.htm); [Cambridge Bible, search excerpt](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/psalms/75.htm))
- **A grim irony:** Maclaren notes "a grim contrast between the images of festivity and hospitality called up by the picture of a host presenting the wine cup to his guests, and the stern compulsion which makes the 'wicked' gulp down the nauseous draught held by God to their reluctant lips." ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-75/))
- **"Red" (foaming) and "fully mixed":** The wine is potent and spiced for pungency. Kidner: "'Well mixed' is a reference to the spices which might be added for pungency; so New English Bible, 'hot with spice'." ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-75/)). Spurgeon adds: "The retribution is terrible, it is blood for blood, foaming vengeance for foaming malice." The "mixture" includes "spices of anger, justice, and incensed mercy." ([Spurgeon](https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps075.php))
- **Drinking to the dregs:** The wicked cannot refuse the cup; God Himself pours it out. Caryl: "They have loved long draughts, and now they shall have one long enough; there is eternity to the bottom." ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-75/)). Spurgeon: "Even to the bitter end must wrath proceed. They must drink on and on for ever… Mark well, it is for all the wicked; all hell for all the ungodly; the dregs for the dregs; bitters for the bitter; wrath for the heirs of wrath." ([Spurgeon](https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps075.php))
- **Gill connects this to Revelation 14:10:** "the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out full strength into the cup of His indignation." The dregs represent everlasting destruction. ([Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/75.htm))
- **Constable adds historical context:** "In some nations kings made convicted criminals drink poisoned wine." ([Constable](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-75.html))

---

## v. 9 — "But I will proclaim Him forever; I will sing praise to the God of Jacob."

- **Contrast with the wicked:** While the wicked are forced to drink wrath, the righteous sing praises. Spurgeon: "Thus will the saints occupy themselves with rehearsing Jehovah's praises, while their foes are drunken with the wine of wrath. They shall chant while the others roar in anguish." ([Spurgeon](https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps075.php))
- **"The God of Jacob":** This is the covenant name, recalling the God who "delivered Jacob from a thousand afflictions" and kept His covenant with the patriarch. ([Spurgeon](https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps075.php))
- **Gill's Christological reading:** He sees these as the words of Christ Himself, who will "declare" the Father's name and purposes, just as in Psalm 22:22. ([Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/75.htm))
- **Constable:** Asaph concludes by praising God publicly and in song for judging His enemies. The psalm has a temple-worship setting. ([Constable](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-75.html))

---

## v. 10 — "All the horns of the wicked I will cut off, but the horns of the righteous will be exalted."

- **God speaks again:** The divine voice returns for the final word, making the psalm end as it began with God's own declaration. This literary inclusio ties the psalm together. ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-75/))
- **"Horns" as power and honour:** Poole: "Their honour and power, which they made an instrument of mischief to oppress good men. A metaphor from horned and mischievous beasts." Clarke: "All their power and influence, will I cut off; and will exalt and extend the power of the righteous." (Both cited in [Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-75/))
- **Spurgeon's final vision:** "Power and liberty being restored to Israel, she begins again to execute justice… Men wore horns in those days as a part of their state, and these, both literally and figuratively, were to be lopped off… This memorable ode may be sung in times of great depression, when prayer has performed her errand at the mercyseat, and when faith is watching for speedy deliverance." ([Spurgeon](https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps075.php))
- **Gill's eschatology:** "The horns of the righteous" ultimately refers to Christ (the singular "righteous one") — the horn of David and the Messiah — and to the saints who will reign with Him. Kimchi, the medieval Jewish commentator, expected this to be fulfilled in the war of Gog and Magog. ([Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/75.htm))
- **NET Bible translation note:** The MT has "I will cut off" (first person, God speaking), which the UBS Text Project gives an "A" rating (high confidence). Some versions read "He will cut off." ([Bible.org / Utley](https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-75))

---

## Points Where Protestant Traditions Differ

### 1. Speaker Identification (Who is speaking and where?)

This is the major exegetical question of the psalm. Ellicott notes: "It is quite clear that the speaker of these words is God Himself, who suddenly, as in Psalm 46:10, breaks in with the announcement of judgment. But how far the Divine utterance extends in the psalm is not quite clear. Some end it with Psalm 75:3; others with Psalm 75:5." ([Ellicott, search excerpt](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/75.htm))

- **Gill (older Baptist)** sees Christ speaking throughout nearly the entire psalm — vv. 2–5 and vv. 9–10 are all the voice of the Son. ([Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/75.htm))
- **Spurgeon (Baptist)** sees God speaking in vv. 2–5 and again in v. 10, with the church/psalmist speaking in vv. 6–9. ([Spurgeon](https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps075.php))
- **Guzik / Enduring Word (Pentecostal/Charismatic)** follows essentially the same division as Spurgeon: God in vv. 2–5 and v. 10, the psalmist in vv. 1, 6–9. ([Enduring Word](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-75/))
- **Constable (Dallas Seminary / Evangelical)** sees God speaking in vv. 2–5 and possibly again in v. 10, with the rest being Asaph. ([Constable](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-75.html))
- **NET Bible (modern scholarship)** marks vv. 2–8 as God's speech (the closing quotation mark falls after v. 8), with v. 9 as the psalmist and v. 10 as God again. ([NET](https://biblehub.com/net/psalms/75.htm))

### 2. Historical Setting: Temporal Judgment or Eschatological?

- **Ellicott (Anglican)** suggests the early Asmonean (Maccabean) period: Mattathias and his sons are those whom God "setteth up," and the "horn" to be cut off is Antiochus Epiphanes (cf. Daniel 8:9). ([Ellicott, search excerpt](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/75.htm))
- **Gill (Baptist)** reads it as referring to the Gospel dispensation, Christ's first and second comings, and the destruction of antichrist (both Pagan and Papal Rome). ([Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/75.htm))
- **Spurgeon (Baptist)** says it is "a song of the second advent, concerning the nearness of the Judge with the cup of wrath." He also sees a possible historical connection to the destruction of Sennacherib's army (2 Kings 19:35). ([Spurgeon](https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps075.php))
- **Constable (Evangelical)** sees it as a communal thanksgiving psalm anticipating a temporal victory in Israel, with the perspective toward the day when God will act in justice. He does not tie it to a specific historical event. ([Constable](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-75.html))

### 3. The "Missing North" in v. 6

Interpretations differ notably:
- **Perowne (Anglican scholarly):** The north is omitted because the Assyrian enemy came from the north — you do not look for help from the direction of the threat. (Cited in [Spurgeon](https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps075.php))
- **Caryl (Puritan):** The north is where promotion *does* come from, because Hebrew *tsaphon* means "hidden" — promotion comes from God's secret, hidden providence. (Cited in [Spurgeon](https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps075.php))
- **NET Bible:** The verse uses Palestinian/Canaanite imagery to express universality. The north may be omitted simply because the psalmist lists three of four compass points as a poetic device meaning "from nowhere on earth." ([Bible.org / Utley](https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-75))

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship

- **NET Bible notes** observe that the MT for v. 2 reads "When I take an appointed time," but the UBS Text Project gives "congregation" a "C" rating (considerable doubt). The imagery of "pillars" (v. 3) and "horns" (vv. 4–5, 10) reflects ancient Near Eastern symbolism. The NET renders v. 6 as universal assertion: victory/help does not come from any earthly direction. ([NET](https://biblehub.com/net/psalms/75.htm); [Bible.org](https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-75))
- **Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges** notes that the cup figure "is a common one" found throughout Jeremiah, Isaiah, Job, and other Psalms (Ps 11:6; 60:3). The "wine is red" is better rendered "foameth" (RV). ([Cambridge, search excerpt](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/psalms/75.htm))
- **Bible.org (Bob Utley)** raises study questions: Does the psalm magnify God as Creator or Judge? Does it look toward temporal or end-time judgment? What do "pillars" signify? He notes the difficulty of knowing when the psalmist is speaking and when he is speaking for God. ([Bible.org](https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-75))

### Catholic and Orthodox Readings

I was unable to fetch pages from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org within the available search and fetch limits. However, Catholic tradition has historically read Psalm 75 in light of the Magnificat (Luke 1:46–53), which echoes its themes of God putting down the mighty and exalting the lowly. The cup imagery in v. 8 would be read in contrast to the Eucharistic cup — the cup of wrath versus the cup of salvation. The Vulgate and Douay-Rheims follow the older "When I shall take a time" / "When I shall receive the assembly" reading.

### Other Views: Prosperity / Word of Faith / Hyper-Grace

No results were found from the searched sites addressing Psalm 75 from these perspectives. The psalm's emphasis on God alone as the source of exaltation and its strong warning against boasting would, in traditional readings, cut against any teaching that presents earthly promotion or self-exaltation as something believers can claim or declare by their own initiative. The repeated theme "God puts down one and exalts another" roots all promotion in God's sovereign will, not human effort or confession — a point that traditional commentators across traditions emphasise.
